title: Azure Regions and Availability Zones
description: Understand Azure regions, availability zones, geographies, and paired regions for building resilient applications.

data.text: Azure's global network of data centers is organized into regions, availability zones, and geographies. Where you place your resources directly affects your application's speed, cost, and reliability.

A **region** is a geographic area containing one or more nearby data centers. When you create a resource, you choose a region. Choosing a region close to your users reduces latency. Not all Azure services are available in every region.

**Availability Zones** are physically separate locations within a region, each with its own power, cooling, and network. Deploying resources across multiple zones protects your application from data center failures. Not every region supports availability zones.

data.caption: How regions, availability zones, and geographies relate to each other
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Geography: Europe] --> B[Region: West Europe]
    A --> C[Region: North Europe]
    B --> D[Availability Zone 1]
    B --> E[Availability Zone 2]
    B --> F[Availability Zone 3]
    D --> G[Data Center]
    E --> H[Data Center]
    F --> I[Data Center]

data.text: A **geography** is a discrete market — such as the United States, Europe, or Asia Pacific — that usually contains two or more regions. Azure pairs regions within a geography for replication. Paired regions are physically separated (at least 300 miles apart) so that a large-scale disaster does not affect both regions.

data.title: Benefits of Paired Regions
items: Platform updates roll out to only one region of a pair at a time
Data replication between paired regions for backup

rows: Host your app close to users

terms.definition: A geographic area containing one or more Azure data centers.
Physically isolated locations within a region, each with independent power and cooling.
A discrete market that contains one or more regions, used for data residency.
Two regions within the same geography that are linked for replication and disaster recovery.

data.text: Check Regions and Zones Before You Deploy

Not every service or VM size is available in every region, and not every region has availability zones. Query the subscription instead of assuming: the `locationInfo` field on a SKU tells you which zones support it.

data.title: List regions and zone support
data.content: The first command lists the regions available to your subscription. The second checks whether a specific VM size is available in zones in West Europe.
data.code:
az account list-locations --output table

az vm list-skus \
  --location westeurope \
  --size Standard_D2s_v5 \
  --query "[].{Name:name, Zones:locationInfo[0].zones}" \
  --output json

data.title: Zone-redundant App Service plan in Bicep
data.content: Zone redundancy requires a premium tier and at least three instances so the platform can spread them across zones.

data.title: Paired regions are not automatic failover
data.text: Azure replicates some platform data between paired regions, but your application, data, and configuration are not failed over for you. You still need a disaster-recovery plan that replicates data, deploys infrastructure to the secondary region, and tests failover. Availability zones protect against a data-center failure inside one region; paired regions protect against a region-wide event.

data.title: Choose Regions Carefully
data.text: Region choice affects latency, cost, and legal compliance. Some Azure services are only available in certain regions. Check the Azure Products by Region page before designing your architecture.
